paragraphs: Information in a graph must travel far enough to connect related nodes, while noisy or repetitive signals need to fade. When a graph changes over time, these demands interact: information accumulated across connections and successive snapshots can become excessive. This paper introduces LAMP, a model that learns how much information to retain and dissipate in snapshot-based dynamic graphs.

LAMP describes information processing through a dynamical systems framework. It combines impulsive neural ordinary differential equations with an antisymmetric parameterization that supports conservative information flow. Alongside that component, learned dissipative dynamics regulate retention across both space and time. The architecture therefore combines mechanisms for carrying information over long distances with mechanisms for controlling its accumulation.

The authors provide theoretical stability guarantees and analyze the model’s representational power. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, particularly for tasks requiring extended-range dependencies. The stated contribution is a way to make memory retention adaptive while preserving stable, expressive graph representations, addressing information buildup as part of the model’s dynamics.
icml-2026-adaptive-memory-retention-in-d.tldr: LAMP learns how to retain and dissipate information in changing graphs, supporting stable representations and long-range dependencies.

paragraphs: Generative Flow Networks learn to construct discrete objects so that higher-reward objects appear more often, in proportion to their rewards. Training requires exploring a potentially enormous graph of intermediate construction states. Learning can be slow if sampled trajectories repeatedly visit regions the model already represents well, even when other valuable regions remain insufficiently explored.

The paper proposes Adaptive Complementary Exploration, or ACE, which gives exploration its own GFlowNet. The canonical GFlowNet learns the desired reward-proportional distribution. A separate exploration GFlowNet searches for high-reward states in areas the canonical model has underexplored. This makes the exploration objective depend on what the main model still needs to discover, while retaining reward as a guide to worthwhile discoveries.

Across the reported experiments, ACE consistently and significantly improves approximation of the target distribution and the discovery rate of diverse high-reward states relative to prior work. These results connect two goals that can otherwise compete for training samples: accurately representing the desired distribution and finding valuable states beyond familiar regions. The approach makes exploration complementary to the main sampler’s current knowledge.
icml-2026-avoid-what-you-know-divergent-.tldr: ACE trains a separate exploration GFlowNet to find rewarding states that the main sampler has not adequately explored.

paragraphs: A neural network trained on tasks in sequence can lose abilities acquired earlier as it adapts to new ones. This paper treats that conflict as a control problem within neural activity. Signals encouraging new learning compete with signals preserving representations from previous tasks, making preservation an active part of the learning dynamics.

The method turns regularization penalties into preservation signals and learns by minimizing the control effort needed to integrate a new task in their presence. At equilibrium, the resulting neural activities generate weight updates that implicitly incorporate the full curvature associated with prior tasks. The authors call this property the continual-natural gradient. It matters because the updates encode that curvature without requiring its explicit storage.

Experiments report that the framework recovers true prior-task curvature, supports task discrimination, and outperforms existing methods on standard benchmarks without replay. The findings support the proposed connection between activity dynamics and the geometry needed to preserve earlier learning. The central result is that a control-based learning process can incorporate prior-task structure into updates without explicitly storing curvature or replaying earlier tasks.
icml-2026-continual-learning-through-con.tldr: This framework uses competing learning and preservation signals to reduce forgetting without replay or explicit storage of prior-task curvature.

paragraphs: This paper studies robust recovery of single-index models when noise has heavy tails and an adversary can corrupt a constant fraction of both inputs and responses. Its goal is to extend efficient recovery beyond monotonic nonlinearities and the special case of phase retrieval. The authors obtain near-linear running time and optimal sample complexity for a broad class of nonlinear, non-monotonic link functions.

The key is a local region of favorable optimization geometry. The paper identifies a sufficient condition for a convex basin around the true parameter whose constant radius does not shrink with dimension. It then introduces Expected Squared Convexity, another sufficient structural condition, under which a spectral initialization lands inside that basin despite the noise and adversarial contamination.

The initialization achieves error O(ε^(1/4)). A subsequent robust gradient descent phase improves this to O(σ√ε), surpassing the spectral initialization’s error barrier. The framework provides efficient recovery guarantees for link functions including GeLU and Swish. These are conditional guarantees built on the identified structural conditions: the contribution is showing how suitable local geometry and robust initialization jointly enable recovery for previously difficult nonlinearities.
icml-2026-convex-basins-in-single-index-.tldr: Sufficient conditions for local convexity and robust initialization enable efficient recovery of broad nonlinear single-index models under strong corruption.

paragraphs: The paper asks which deeply structured prediction problems neural networks can efficiently learn. It studies supervised learning with an unknown hierarchy of labels. Labels at the simplest level are simple functions of the input; labels at later levels are simple functions of labels already available at earlier levels. The hierarchy therefore exposes a sequence of intermediate learning targets.

The authors show that residual networks trained with layerwise stochastic gradient descent can efficiently learn this model class. The class includes models that require polynomial depth to express, extending beyond previously established learnable classes computable by logarithmic-depth circuits. This is a result about learning genuinely deep hierarchical computations under the stated label structure.

The paper also explores why such supervision might arise naturally. A teacher’s granular labels can reveal pieces of an internal reasoning process. In a simplified model where teachers have partial awareness of their internal logic, the authors formalize how a learnable hierarchy emerges. They suggest this could eventually help explain deep learning’s success; that broader explanatory role is presented as a possibility rather than an established general account.
icml-2026-deep-networks-learn-deep-hiera.tldr: Layerwise training of residual networks can efficiently learn a class of label hierarchies containing computations that require polynomial depth.

paragraphs: Language model distillation trains a student to match a teacher’s output probabilities. The usual Kullback-Leibler divergence can concentrate the learning signal on outcomes the teacher already considers most likely. Lower-probability alternatives may contain useful information, yet contribute relatively little to the student’s training objective. This paper changes how those two parts of the distribution influence learning.

The proposed divergence separates the teacher’s top-K predictions from the remaining probability tail. By decoupling their contributions, it reduces the dominance of the most likely outcomes and increases the tail’s influence. The method maintains the same computational profile as standard KL divergence, so emphasizing less-probable predictions does not require a more expensive divergence calculation.

Experiments report competitive mathematical reasoning performance across datasets in both pre-training and supervised distillation of decoder models. The authors also report that the distillation process can handle large datasets on modest academic budgets, substantially reducing the costs typically associated with large-scale distillation. The findings support treating the teacher’s broader distribution as a useful source of supervision, beyond its strongest predictions.
icml-2026-dont-ignore-the-tail-decoupled.tldr: A decoupled distillation objective gives lower-probability teacher predictions more influence while retaining KL divergence’s computational profile.

paragraphs: Choosing how much training data to draw from each domain changes a model’s performance across those domains. Existing empirical scaling laws describe these effects, but the paper seeks an explanation for their shape. It extends theoretical ideas from standard neural scaling laws to training mixtures containing several domains.

The framework assumes that domains share fundamental skills while differing in specialized skills. Under this picture, two mechanisms govern domain losses. Capacity Competition reflects how finite model capacity links learning across domains: allocating capacity to one part of the mixture affects the others. Noise Reduction explains why optimal mixture weights shift toward domains that are harder to learn, reducing overall noise.

Empirical evaluations show lower mean relative fitting error and better-performing training mixtures than existing baselines, using substantially fewer free parameters than earlier empirical laws. Parameters fitted at smaller scales also predict effective mixtures at larger, unseen scales. These results suggest that the proposed mechanisms can support practical mixture selection as well as explanation, with extrapolation across scale being a central reported finding.
icml-2026-explaining-data-mixing-scaling.tldr: A framework based on shared skills, finite capacity, and noise reduction explains data-mixture losses and predicts effective mixtures at unseen scales.

paragraphs: Inverse design starts with desired performance and seeks design parameters that achieve it. Generative methods can produce multiple candidate solutions, but adapting conditional flow matching by pairing performance labels with design parameters makes training sensitive to arbitrary coordinate ordering and scaling. This paper introduces Diagonal Flow Matching to stabilize that learning setup.

Its zero-anchoring strategy pairs design coordinates with noise and performance labels with zero. The resulting learning problem is provably invariant to coordinate permutations. Across evaluated problems with design dimensions up to 784, the method achieves substantially lower round-trip error than conditional flow matching and invertible neural network baselines, including order-of-magnitude improvements on several benchmarks.

The authors also develop two uncertainty measures built into the architecture: Zero-Deviation and Self-Consistency. These support choosing among generated candidates, withholding unreliable predictions, and detecting targets outside the training distribution. The measures consistently outperform ensemble and general-purpose alternatives across the evaluated tasks. Validation spans airfoils, gas turbine combustors, analytical problems, photonics, and image statistics, connecting the method’s coordinate treatment to both design generation and practical reliability decisions.
icml-2026-generative-inverse-design-with.tldr: Diagonal Flow Matching makes inverse-design learning invariant to coordinate permutations and supplies uncertainty measures for candidate selection and abstention.

paragraphs: Language model samplers often discard some next-token options before sampling, balancing variety against coherence. Most such rules primarily use probabilities or entropy. This paper introduces Top-W, which also considers relationships between tokens in embedding space. It uses a Wasserstein distance defined through that geometry to keep the truncated distribution close to the original.

The objective balances the probability mass retained with the entropy of the kept tokens. For a subset update with fixed potentials, the authors derive a simple optimal structure: depending on that trade-off, the selected set contains either a single token or a one-dimensional prefix identifiable by a linear scan. The implementation uses efficient geometric potentials and alternates updates while preserving the usual truncation-and-sampling interface.

Experiments across four benchmarks and three instruction-tuned models report consistent improvements over prior state-of-the-art decoding approaches. Gains appear in accuracy-oriented evaluations and in creativity assessed by judges on open-ended generation. The findings support using token geometry as an additional guide to selection, with the fixed-potential theoretical result helping make the proposed decoding procedure computationally practical.
icml-2026-geometry-aware-decoding-with-w.tldr: Top-W uses token-embedding geometry alongside probability mass and entropy to choose which tokens remain available for sampling.

paragraphs: A prior probabilistic account connects hallucination in calibrated language models to missing mass: the portion of the source distribution absent from training data. This paper asks what property underlies that connection and whether abandoning calibration would avoid the problem. It introduces innovation, a measure of how often a model produces outputs outside its training data.

Within the probabilistic framework, the authors show that the previously identified condition for hallucination implies innovation. They then establish an almost characterization: hallucination implies innovation, while innovation implies hallucination with high probability. The qualification matters because the converse is probabilistic; the result does not label every individual output absent from training data as a hallucination.

The paper derives lower bounds on hallucination rates from innovation rates. By connecting innovation back to missing mass, it also obtains new missing-mass-based lower bounds extending the earlier results. The contribution is to identify a simpler property through which to study unavoidable hallucination, shifting attention from calibration alone toward the model’s tendency to produce material beyond its observed training examples.
icml-2026-innovation-an-almost-character.tldr: In a probabilistic framework, producing outputs beyond training data almost characterizes hallucination and yields new lower bounds on its rate.

paragraphs: Causal analysis sometimes needs an entire function describing how outcomes change under interventions, rather than a single effect estimate. Quantifying uncertainty over that function is challenging. This paper proposes a Gaussian-process-based approach that learns uncertainty about interventional functions from observational data, allowing uncertainty to accompany the estimated relationship across interventions.

The method builds on a representation of interventional functions as inner products of observational functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. It constructs suitable Gaussian process priors for those functions and infers their posteriors. The construction produces closed-form posterior moments and tractable training and inference, while avoiding pathologies associated with earlier Gaussian process priors for functions in this setting.

The authors also derive a practical procedure to calibrate posterior coverage, addressing how uncertainty statements align with the quantities they aim to cover. Evaluations include synthetic benchmarks, causal Bayesian optimization, and a large real dataset. The method improves uncertainty quantification while remaining competitive in causal effect estimation, indicating that its main empirical advantage concerns the quality of uncertainty alongside the estimated effects.
icml-2026-interventional-processes-for-c.tldr: A Gaussian process construction provides tractable uncertainty estimates for entire causal intervention functions, with a procedure for calibrating posterior coverage.

paragraphs: A language model can spend substantial computation completing a long reasoning trace that ultimately leads to an incorrect answer. Dynamic abstention addresses this by allowing the model to stop partway through generation. This paper develops a formal basis for deciding when to quit, extending beyond rules that only decide whether to answer before or after the full response is generated.

The authors model abstention as an explicit action in a regularized reinforcement learning framework. A reward assigned to abstaining controls the trade-off between computation and information. Their rule compares the value of the current reasoning state with that reward and stops when the value falls below it. Under general conditions, they prove that this rule strictly outperforms natural baselines.

Because applying the rule requires a value estimate, the paper also derives an efficient approximation method. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks support the theory and show improved selective accuracy over existing approaches. Selective accuracy concerns correctness among responses the system chooses to provide, making the stopping decision part of the method’s performance rather than merely an after-generation filter.
icml-2026-knowing-when-to-quit-a-princip.tldr: A reinforcement learning analysis yields a value-based rule for stopping unpromising reasoning traces, with improved selective accuracy in mathematical reasoning experiments.

paragraphs: Long-context language models store past attention keys and values, so memory usage increases with sequence length. Compressing this cache requires deciding which tokens to retain. ManifoldKV scores tokens by their keys’ Euclidean distance from the key centroid. Unlike cosine-based scoring, this captures differences in magnitude as well as direction, preserving cues that can distinguish salient tokens.

On RULER at 4K–16K contexts with 20% compression, the method reaches 95.7% accuracy, matching the best geometric baseline overall. Its advantage becomes clearer in multi-key retrieval: at 50% compression, it achieves 92.4% on 3-key NIAH compared with KeyDiff’s 77.0%. To address deterioration of a global centroid at longer contexts, the authors introduce WindowedManifoldKV, which restores accuracy to 84.3% at 64K context with 25% compression.

Further evaluations report gains on LongBench, HELMET, and InfiniteBench. Across six model architectures, the authors find that the best distance metric depends on the geometry of key norms. The findings therefore support magnitude-aware scoring while identifying an actual qualification: metric choice depends on the model’s key geometry. Both variants require no additional training.
icml-2026-manifoldkv-training-free-kv-ca.tldr: ManifoldKV uses magnitude-sensitive Euclidean scoring to retain cache tokens, with a windowed variant addressing failures at very long contexts.

paragraphs: Enforcing an output constraint by masking invalid next tokens can distort a language model’s distribution over complete valid outputs. This paper targets sampling from the model’s distribution conditioned on satisfying the constraint. Sequential Monte Carlo can reduce the distortion, but its effectiveness depends on the proposals and potential functions used to guide candidate sequences.

The authors construct globally constrained decoding proposals from constraints represented as finite automata. They express those automata as tensor operations suitable for efficient GPU execution. They then exploit a shared circuit structure with hidden Markov models, combining the circuits to produce probabilistic globally constrained proposals. These incorporate both the logical requirements and probabilistic information about the desired output distribution.

Evaluations cover function calling, generation with keyword requirements, and SQL generation. Within the same sequential Monte Carlo setup, the proposed methods converge toward the target distribution faster and use significantly fewer particles than locally constrained proposals. The result concerns the quality and efficiency of constrained sampling: looking beyond immediate token legality gives the sampling process more useful guidance toward complete valid outputs.
icml-2026-mitigating-bias-in-locally-con.tldr: GPU-friendly global constraint proposals help sequential Monte Carlo sample valid language-model outputs with less bias and fewer particles.

paragraphs: Weight-space networks take the parameters of other neural networks as their inputs. Leading designs respect permutations of those parameters, an architectural choice intended to improve generalization. This paper examines whether that symmetry restricts what they can represent. The analysis must account for both operations on the numerical weights and operations on the functions those weights describe.

The authors develop a systematic expressivity theory and prove that all prominent permutation-equivariant weight-space networks have equivalent expressive power. Under mild, natural assumptions on the input weights, they establish universality in both weight-space and function-space settings. They also characterize exceptional regimes where universality fails, making the assumptions part of the expressivity result.

The theory guides small modifications to existing models that produce a reported 34% improvement over prior state-of-the-art performance. That empirical finding demonstrates practical relevance for the analysis without making universality itself a performance guarantee. Together, the results clarify the representational capabilities shared by prominent architectures and show how understanding their boundaries can inform changes to working weight-space models.
icml-2026-on-the-expressive-power-of-per.tldr: A unified theory establishes equivalent expressivity and conditional universality for prominent permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, guiding effective architectural changes.

paragraphs: Self-distillation retrains a model using a mixture of original labels and predictions from a teacher with the same architecture and training data. This paper analyzes that process for ridge regression while allowing the mixing weight to be any real number. That freedom matters because the best mixture can involve a negative weight, particularly when the teacher is over-regularized.

Conditional on the training data and without distributional assumptions, the authors prove strict improvement in any squared prediction risk, including out-of-distribution risk, wherever the teacher’s risk derivative with respect to regularization is nonzero. The guarantee concerns the optimally mixed student. The paper characterizes that optimal weight through the risk derivative, explicitly connecting the benefit to how the teacher’s risk changes with regularization.

The authors also derive exact risk asymptotics for proportionally growing problems with general anisotropic covariance and deterministic signals. For practical use, they propose a consistent one-shot estimator of the mixing weight that avoids grid search, sample splitting, and refitting. Experiments using real datasets and pretrained neural network features support both the theoretical analysis and the tuning method.
icml-2026-optimal-unconstrained-self-dis.tldr: Optimally weighted self-distillation strictly improves ridge regression wherever teacher risk is nonstationary in regularization, and the optimal weight can be negative.

paragraphs: Automatic seizure detection must work across patients and clinical settings, yet strong reported results often fail to transfer to unseen populations. This study evaluates that gap through a competition collecting 28 approaches, ranging from engineered features to deep learning. All were tested on a strictly held-out private dataset containing 4,360 hours of continuous EEG from 65 subjects, with expert annotations of seizure events.

Using the SzCORE event-based evaluation framework, the best algorithm achieved an F1 score of 32%, with 37% sensitivity and 29% precision. Performance varied substantially across approaches and patients. Algorithms with the highest overall F1 scores did not have the most consistent rankings across subjects, showing that a strong aggregate result could coexist with vulnerability on particular patients.

The independent evaluation exposed a gap between self-reported efficacy and held-out performance, even though the best algorithm surpassed prior methods in the reported comparison. The evaluation infrastructure becomes a continuously open benchmark supporting ongoing submissions and additional private datasets. Clinical centers can also use it on their own EEG data, extending standardized evaluation beyond a single competition.
icml-2026-quantifying-the-generalization.tldr: A private EEG benchmark reveals substantial generalization failures and patient-level instability across 28 seizure-detection approaches.

paragraphs: Planning with a simulator requires estimating state values while limiting simulator calls. This paper studies how the local smoothness used by a planning estimator controls that cost. It shows that, for SmoothCruiser-type planners, the sample-complexity exponent depends on the order β of the local Taylor remainder, yielding complexity proportional to ε^−(2+2/(β−1)), up to logarithmic factors.

A first-order estimator with a quadratic remainder recovers the existing ε^−4 dependence. A second-order estimator with a cubic remainder improves it to ε^−3. To achieve this regime, the authors smooth the Bellman backup over action distributions using optimal transport. The resulting backup has a closed form, a policy gradient, and a Lipschitz Hessian; its quadratic correction admits an unbiased cross-product estimator.

The resulting SecondOrderSmoothCruiser achieves ε^−3 oracle complexity, up to logarithmic factors, for fixed optimal-transport parameters. The paper also provides explicit bounds on the bias separating optimal-transport-smoothed, entropy-regularized, and unregularized objectives. Those bounds matter because the computational guarantee applies to a smoothed planning objective, and smoothing changes the value being estimated.
icml-2026-second-order-smooth-planning-w.tldr: Optimal-transport smoothing enables a second-order planner with ε^−3 oracle complexity for fixed smoothing parameters, improving the earlier ε^−4 dependence.

paragraphs: Indoor visual localization estimates a camera’s pose from what it sees. Repeating that process across an image sequence can refine the estimate, but conventional environment representations may require large image collections or point clouds. SG2Loc instead uses a compact 3D scene graph, with objects represented by coarse meshes and edges describing spatial relationships.

For each incoming image, the system extracts semantic features from image patches to predict object identities. A particle filter maintains candidate camera poses. Each candidate projects the graph’s object meshes into the image and determines which object identities should be visible in each patch. Agreement between the observed patch features and the graph’s object features sets the candidate’s weight.

As additional images arrive, the filter incorporates their evidence and refines the pose estimate. Evaluations on real-world datasets show substantially reduced storage while maintaining performance. The contribution lies in making a compact object-based environment representation useful for sequential localization: coarse geometry supplies visibility predictions, semantic matching scores those predictions, and the image sequence progressively improves the estimate.
icml-2026-sg2loc-sequential-visual-local.tldr: SG2Loc localizes a camera over time by matching image semantics against a compact 3D object graph within a particle filter.

paragraphs: Some geometric observations, such as tangent vectors or local frames, belong to spaces attached to different points on a manifold. Averaging them requires transporting them into one reference space. This paper develops finite-sample concentration theory for those transported averages, accounting for geometric effects that do not appear when every observation starts in the same vector space.

The authors derive dimension-free Hoeffding- and Bernstein-type bounds. When shortest paths to the reference point are not unique, the transport can depend on the chosen path. They isolate the resulting deterministic holonomy bias and quantify it through curvature and loop geometry, including sharp closed-form expressions for the tangent bundle of a round sphere.

The error decomposition separates random fluctuations, which decrease at the usual inverse-square-root rate in sample size, from a curvature-driven error floor that more observations cannot remove. Minimax lower bounds confirm that both components are unavoidable in the analyzed setting. The paper also supplies a robust median-of-means estimator for heavy-tailed observations and a central limit theorem in the reference space, with controlled sphere experiments supporting the predictions.
icml-2026-sharp-concentration-bounds-for.tldr: New concentration bounds separate sampling error from path-dependent geometric bias when averaging observations transported across a manifold.

paragraphs: Ultra-high-resolution remote sensing images combine enormous spatial coverage with crucial details that may occupy only a few pixels. Feeding all that visual information into a vision-language model creates a large token burden. Downsampling, dense tiling, and global token pruning can lose query-relevant details or make computational demands difficult to control.

UHR-BAT compresses visual tokens under a strict context budget, using the text query to guide selection. It estimates token importance at multiple spatial scales, allowing the requested information to influence what is retained. Region-wise preservation and merging then reduce redundant tokens while respecting the regional structure of the image. These components address both the search for small relevant evidence and the cost of representing the broader scene.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks. The stated result supports combining query guidance with regional compression for this setting, where the largest visual structures need not contain the most useful evidence. Budget awareness is part of the framework’s design, tying token selection directly to the available context capacity while seeking to preserve the details needed to answer the query.
icml-2026-uhr-bat-budget-aware-token-com.tldr: UHR-BAT uses query-guided, multiscale token selection and regional merging to process huge remote sensing images within a strict context budget.

paragraphs: Optimal transport typically uses a fixed cost function to return one transport plan. Real data contain noise and variability, so uncertainty over possible plans can matter as well. Existing sampling-based approaches represent that uncertainty, but the paper identifies their computational cost and limited scalability as obstacles to larger applications.

The proposed Sinkhorn-parameterized Variational Inference approximates a posterior distribution over transport plans. Its central step treats the Sinkhorn map as a differentiable reparameterization of entropic plans. This allows flexible generative models, including normalizing flows, to represent distributions of plans while enforcing the required marginal constraints. Those constraints remain part of the construction rather than being left to an unconstrained approximation.

Experiments show that the method matches the quality of computationally intensive sampling approaches at a fraction of their cost and scales to large problems. The contribution is a tractable way to retain uncertainty over transport decisions: a generative approximation supplies flexibility, while the Sinkhorn parameterization keeps its outputs within the constrained family of transport plans.
icml-2026-variational-inference-for-unce.tldr: A differentiable Sinkhorn parameterization enables scalable variational uncertainty estimates over transport plans while enforcing their marginal constraints.

paragraphs: Reasoning video object segmentation requires interpreting a linguistic reference and identifying the corresponding object at pixel level across a video. Difficult references can depend on both fine visual details and events separated in time. VideoSEG-O3 addresses the limitations of reasoning from fixed initial inputs by allowing the system to seek additional visual evidence over multiple turns.

Its temporal-spatial reasoning process progressively identifies useful time intervals and keyframes, moving from a broad view toward the details needed for segmentation. A separated thinking trace organizes temporal, spatial, and linguistic reasoning. The authors also introduce VTS-CoT, a dataset of detailed reasoning trajectories used to initialize this behavior before reinforcement learning.

During reinforcement learning, SEG-aware logit calibration incorporates pixel-level segmentation feedback into token-level logits. This gives the policy a signal about the quality of its segmentation beyond the text probability assigned to the segmentation token. Experiments across eight mainstream benchmarks report advanced performance, with particular strengths on long-horizon and complex reasoning tasks. The findings support combining active evidence gathering with training feedback that reflects the actual localization outcome.
icml-2026-videoseg-o3-a-multi-turn-reinf.tldr: VideoSEG-O3 iteratively gathers video evidence and uses segmentation-aware reinforcement learning to improve reasoning-based object localization.

paragraphs: Reasoning hallucinations can sound coherent while contradicting the supplied context or underlying facts. This paper studies their emergence in decoder-only Transformers through a graph-search perspective on next-token prediction. Entities serve as nodes, and learned transitions act as edges, allowing different kinds of reasoning to be described in terms of paths through learned relationships.

In this account, reasoning from a supplied context searches a sampled subgraph under contextual constraints. Queries without such context instead depend on memorized structure in the underlying graph. The authors identify path reuse as an early-training mechanism: memorized knowledge takes precedence over the constraints of the current context, producing an unsupported conclusion.

They identify a second mechanism, path compression, in later training. Frequently used multistep paths become compressed into shortcut edges. Together, reuse and compression explain how learned transitions can generate reasoning hallucinations at different stages of training. The paper presents the two mechanisms as a unified account and connects them to familiar downstream behaviors, distinguishing context-overriding memory from the formation of shortcuts through repeatedly traversed reasoning paths.
icml-2026-when-do-hallucinations-arise-a.tldr: A graph-search account links reasoning hallucinations to early reuse of memorized paths and later compression of multistep paths into shortcuts.

paragraphs: Tokenization compresses input into the units a language model processes, yet its boundaries often remain hardcoded outside end-to-end learning. Earlier approaches have brought boundary selection into the model using heuristics or straight-through estimates that treat discrete choices as continuous during optimization. This paper investigates learning those boundaries directly as discrete decisions.

The authors use score-function estimates to optimize boundary selection for lower loss. They report tighter theoretical guarantees than straight-through estimates because the objective directly addresses the discrete boundary problem. Making this practical requires controlling estimator variance. Techniques from reinforcement learning, including time discounting, are found necessary to reduce that variance sufficiently in the proposed method.

At the 100-million-parameter scale, the resulting approach outperforms previously proposed straight-through estimates in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. The finding establishes a practical route to learned token boundaries at the tested scale, connecting a theoretically better-matched optimization method with the variance reduction needed to use it. The contribution concerns making tokenization itself trainable as part of the model’s learning process.
icml-2026-you-can-learn-tokenization-end.tldr: Reinforcement-learning variance reduction makes direct optimization of discrete token boundaries practical, outperforming straight-through estimates at the 100-million-parameter scale.
